job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based on the supplied text, these are potential gaps and drafting problems—not conclusions that a court would necessarily adopt. Some are express exceptions or policy choices rather than unintended loopholes.

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel threshold permits fleet splitting.** The 10,000-metric-ton threshold applies to a “single vessel,” without aggregating vessels under common ownership or control. Companies could divide recovery among multiple vessels, although section 2(1)(B) might capture those operations if the Secretary makes a determination.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—Exactly 10,000 tons is outside the automatic prohibition.** The definition covers recovery of “more than” 10,000 metric tons, leaving operations at or below that amount outside subparagraph (A). There is no separate limit on cumulative recovery across multiple years.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Per year” lacks a measurement period.** The text does not specify a calendar year, rolling 12-month period, or operating year. That creates uncertainty about staggered production and when an operation crosses the threshold and becomes unlawful.

4. **Section 2(1)(A)—Tonnage measurement is unspecified.** The bill does not say whether the threshold measures wet material, dry material, mineral content, or material actually retained. Different measurement methods could produce materially different compliance results.

5. **Section 2(1)(A)—The depth boundary leaves shallower mining outside the automatic prohibition.** Recovery at exactly 200 meters or shallower does not qualify under subparagraph (A), regardless of scale. The bill also supplies no method for measuring depth or handling operations spanning the boundary.

6. **Section 2(1)(A)—Recovery by non-vessel systems is uncertain.** The phrase “by a single vessel” does not clearly address seabed installations, remotely operated collectors, or systems dividing collection and lifting among several platforms. Such arrangements could contest coverage under subparagraph (A), though subparagraph (B) remains a possible backstop.

7. **Section 2(1)—“Commercial” is not an economic test.** Despite the label, the definition does not require sale, profit, or commercial intent. Large research operations could therefore qualify while smaller profit-making operations escape subparagraph (A), creating a mismatch between the bill’s terminology and its operative scope.

8. **Section 2(1)(B)—The responsible Secretary is undefined.** The bill never identifies which Secretary may determine that an activity presents comparable ecosystem risks. Section 6’s express reference to the Secretary of State does not clearly resolve who administers section 2.

9. **Section 2(1)(B)—The risk standard lacks usable benchmarks.** “Risks” and “comparable” are undefined, and subparagraph (A) encompasses operations of widely varying scale and impact. The provision gives no criteria for comparing likelihood, severity, duration, or geographic extent of harm.

10. **Section 2(1)(B)—The determination process is missing.** The bill specifies no procedure, deadline, publication requirement, or effective date for risk determinations. Operators could argue that activities outside subparagraph (A) remain permissible until a valid determination covers them; unclear notice also creates due-process concerns, especially for criminal enforcement.

11. **Sections 2(1)(B) and 5—Broad administrative discretion invites legal challenge.** Allowing an unidentified Secretary to designate “any activity” as prohibited, backed by substantial civil and criminal penalties, raises questions about statutory boundaries and fair notice. A delegation or vagueness challenge is possible, but its success would depend on implementation and judicial interpretation.

12. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a)—“U.S. person” excludes important entity types.** The definition does not expressly cover LLCs, partnerships, trusts, unincorporated associations, or corporations organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law. Those entities could argue that their mining outside the United States is not covered.

13. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries are not attributed to U.S. owners.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary is not itself a “U.S. person,” and the bill contains no ownership, control, or anti-evasion rule. U.S. owners’ direct participation might still create liability, but ownership alone is not expressly prohibited.

14. **Section 3(a)—The territorial reach is unclear.** “In the United States” is undefined, leaving questions about territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, the continental shelf, and U.S.-flagged vessels abroad. The bill does not clearly establish coverage of foreign operators in those settings.

15. **Section 3(a)—Supporting activities are not expressly prohibited.** The text bans “engag[ing] in” mining but does not separately address financing, contracting, equipment supply, transport, processing, or purchasing mined material. Some conduct might fall within direct participation or generally applicable criminal rules, but the bill provides no tailored coverage.

16. **Section 3(b)—Exploration licenses exempt mining, not merely exploration.** The exception applies to “mining conducted under an exploration license,” with no express tonnage limit or restriction to noncommercial work. An operator could argue that substantial recovery is exempt if its pre-enactment license authorizes that activity.

17. **Section 3(b)—Qualifying licenses and issuers are undefined.** The bill does not identify the licensing authority, jurisdiction, or standards required for an “exploration license.” Operators could seek exemption based on foreign or other licenses Congress may not have intended to recognize.

18. **Section 3(b)—Grandfathering has no express limits on later changes.** The exception does not address renewals, transfers, amendments, expanded sites, additional vessels, or increased production. Operators could argue that a pre-enactment license continues to shelter an expanded or transferred operation, depending on the license’s terms.

19. **Section 3(c)—Environmental assessment is an uncapped exception.** The text sets no volume, duration, necessity, approval, or independent-review requirements for assessment activities. An operator could characterize large-scale recovery as environmental assessment.

20. **Section 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities are unresolved.** The exception does not require environmental assessment to be the sole or primary purpose, or prohibit selling recovered minerals. An operation combining assessment with commercial production could claim exemption.

21. **Sections 2(3) and 4—The registry misses vessels capable of prohibited mining.** Only vessels exceeding 5,000 gross tons must register; exactly 5,000-ton and smaller vessels are excluded even if they recover more than 10,000 metric tons annually. This is a monitoring gap, not an exemption from section 3.

22. **Sections 2(3) and 4—Equipment and operator definitions are missing.** “Equipped for” recovery does not clearly address temporary equipment, modular systems, or vessels performing only part of a recovery operation. “Operator” is also undefined, allowing owners, charterers, and contractors to dispute who must register and report.

23. **Section 4(a)—Registration lacks deadlines and jurisdictional limits.** The bill does not specify when registration must occur or whether it must precede operations. “Each covered vessel” also lacks an express U.S. nexus, creating uncertainty about its application to foreign vessels operating entirely abroad.

24. **Section 4(b)—Reports need not provide essential compliance information.** “Describing” recovery activities does not expressly require tonnage, depth, location, license details, assessment justification, or identification of related vessels. Operator certification is not accompanied by recordkeeping, independent verification, or audit requirements.

25. **Sections 4 and 5—Registry violations lack express penalties.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3, not failures to register or report under section 4. Moreover, the reporting duty applies to “registered” operators, giving an unregistered operator a textual argument that the reporting requirement has not attached, although registration remains mandatory.

26. **Sections 3–5—The enforcement framework is incomplete.** The bill does not expressly identify an enforcement agency or provide inspection, subpoena, seizure, stop-work, injunction, or penalty-assessment procedures. Existing authorities might supply some mechanisms, but the text leaves their availability and coordination uncertain.

27. **Sections 2(1)(A) and 5(a)—Daily penalties are difficult to calculate against an annual threshold.** The bill does not explain whether violations begin only after a vessel exceeds 10,000 tons or extend to earlier recovery days in that year. That uncertainty affects both potential liability and fair notice.

28. **Sections 5(a) and 8—Penalty timing conflicts with the delayed effective date.** Civil penalties expressly cover violations occurring on or after enactment, while the Act does not take effect until 180 days later. This creates ambiguity about the intervening period; it does not clearly establish an enforceable prohibition before the effective date.

29. **Section 8—The 180-day delay permits continued operations and restructuring.** Unless another law prohibits them, companies may continue mining before this Act takes effect and reorganize their operations during that period. Newly issued licenses would not qualify for section 3(b), whose cutoff is enactment rather than the effective date.

30. **Section 6—International negotiations do not close foreign-operator gaps.** The Secretary of State must “seek to negotiate,” not secure an agreement or implement foreign prohibitions. The 18-month language also does not clearly distinguish a deadline to initiate negotiations from a deadline to conclude them.

31. **Section 7(a)—The early-termination standard is underspecified.** The bill does not define “serious harm,” identify the required report’s scope, or specify whether findings must address particular technologies, locations, or operating conditions. A finding about limited circumstances could be offered as grounds to end the prohibition generally.

32. **Section 7(a)—No National Academies report is commissioned.** The bill relies on a report without directing anyone to obtain it, funding it, or setting a deadline. That omission could obstruct the contemplated review process rather than provide a loophole for operators.

33. **Section 7(b)—The sunset overrides continued environmental uncertainty.** The entire Act expires after ten years without requiring an agreement, a National Academies report, or a congressional finding of safety. Companies could resume activity prohibited solely by this Act after expiration, subject to other applicable law.

34. **Sections 7(a)–(b)—Termination and surviving obligations are unclear.** Section 7(a) ends the section 3 prohibition through a joint resolution, while section 7(b) ends the entire Act automatically, leaving different consequences for registration and reporting. There is no express transition provision for pending enforcement matters; generally applicable federal savings law may preserve incurred penalties, so expiration should not be described as automatically erasing liability.
